cards.back: A single force equivalent to a distributed load for force and moment balance.
Whether equilibrium equations are sufficient to solve all support reactions without deformation compatibility.
Axial force divided by cross-sectional area, with sign convention for tension or compression.
Change in length divided by original length for a uniaxial specimen.
A geometric condition that connected members must satisfy together; rigid end plates impose equal axial extension on parallel bars.
For a redundant elastic assembly, combine force balance, geometric fit of displacements, and each member's force–deformation relation.
A uniform bar has k = AE/L. For connected parallel bars with common extension δ, Fᵢ = kᵢδ and total load P = ΣFᵢ.
The line in a bent beam where longitudinal normal strain and stress are zero in the elementary model.
A geometric section property governing torsional response of a shaft.
Allowable capacity divided by modeled demand under a specified failure mode.
Progressive damage under repeated or fluctuating loading, potentially below monotonic strength.
σ = My/I, maximum at the outer surface; I(hollow circle) = (π/4)(r_o⁴ − r_i⁴).
Axial P/A adds to bending stress where both act in the same direction.
SF = strength/stress for a named criterion and load case; bone is weaker in tension and fatigue.
Material far from the axis raises I; stiff implants take load from bone.
ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0; take moments about the point where the most unknowns act.
Muscle force = load moment / muscle lever arm, often many times the load.
Only F sin θ creates a moment; F cos θ compresses the joint.
d_muscle/d_load < 1 trades force for speed and range of motion.
K_t = σ_max/σ_nom depends only on geometry and loading; a small circular hole in a wide plate under tension has K_t = 3.
K_t = 1 + 2a/b = 1 + 2√(a/ρ), with a perpendicular to the load; a smaller root radius ρ raises K_t.
Ductile parts redistribute stress by yielding, so the net-section stress governs static strength; brittle parts fracture at the peak; for fatigue use K_f = 1 + q(K_t − 1).
Use the area left after the hole: σ_net = F/((w − d)t); the gross area underestimates the stress.
σ_a = (σ_max − σ_min)/2, σ_m = (σ_max + σ_min)/2, R = σ_min/σ_max; fatigue lives are reported against the amplitude with the mean and R stated.
σ_a = σ_f′ (2N_f)^b, so N_f = ½(σ_a/σ_f′)^(1/b); with b = −0.10 a 10% lower amplitude gives 2.87 times the life.
Goodman: σ_a/σ_e + σ_m/σ_u = 1/n. Miner: D = Σ n_i/N_i, failure near D = 1 but with wide scatter.
Lives scatter log-normally; test several specimens per level, report mean log N and spread, and treat run-outs as censored; many materials have no endurance limit.
P_cr = π²EI/(KL)²: an instability limit set by stiffness (E, I) and length, not by yield strength.
K = 1 pinned–pinned, 0.5 fixed–fixed, about 0.7 fixed–pinned, 2 fixed–free; the load scales as 1/(KL)².
λ = KL/r with r = √(I/A) (d/4 for a solid circle); σ_cr = π²E/λ²; Euler applies when λ is above π√(E/σ_y), otherwise yielding governs.
For a solid circle P_cr scales with d⁴/L²: doubling d gives 16 times, doubling L gives one quarter. Real maxima fall below the Euler value because of imperfections.
σθ = (σx+σy)/2 + (σx−σy)/2 cos2θ + τxy sin2θ; σx+σy is invariant under rotation.
σ1,2 = centre ± R with centre (σx+σy)/2 and R = √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²]; tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx−σy); the maximum in-plane shear is R.
A physical rotation θ is a rotation 2θ on the circle; principal planes are the ends of the horizontal diameter.
Tresca: max(|σ1|, |σ2|, |σ1−σ2|) = σ_y. von Mises: √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²) = σ_y. Both are for ductile, isotropic materials; shear yield is σ_y/2 or σ_y/√3.
Cantilever tip load PL³/(3EI); cantilever uniform load wL⁴/(8EI); simply supported centre load PL³/(48EI); simply supported uniform load 5wL⁴/(384EI).
I = bh³/12 with h in the direction of the load; the stiffness of a three-point bend is k = 48EI/L³ = 4Ebh³/L³ and the maximum stress is 3PL/(2bh²).
E = L³m/(4bh³) from the slope m = P/δ; thickness enters as a cube, so a 5% thickness error is about a 15% modulus error.
Superposition needs linear material and small deflection; short, thick beams need a shear correction; check span-to-thickness (about 16 or more) and that the supports do not indent.
P_f = 1 − exp[−(V/V₀)(σ/σ₀)^m]; at σ = σ₀ and V = V₀ the failure probability is 63.2%.
m measures scatter, not strength: larger m means a narrower distribution; many ceramics have m of about 5 to 20, and an estimate from a handful of specimens is very uncertain.
σ = σ₀[−ln(1 − P_f)]^(1/m) for the reference volume; a 1% failure probability at m = 10 is about 63% of σ₀.
For the same P_f, σ₂/σ₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(1/m); a lower m means a larger penalty for volume; the model does not apply to ductile yielding.
Count specimens and failures per level, average the logarithm of the life, and keep run-outs visible as censored.
Regress mean log life on log stress amplitude; the slope is 1/b for Basquin's law, so b = 1/slope.
A run-out lasted at least to the cutoff; dropping it or counting it as a failure at the cutoff both bias the life low.
A line through a few tested levels does not support a predicted life well below the lowest tested stress, and the median is not a design life because of scatter.
It applies one load once to a new, dry specimen; service applies millions of cycles to a wet, warm, degrading and creeping one, through struts that carry many times the nominal stress.
With b about −0.08, a 15% loss of strength divides the fatigue life by about 7.6; a thin life margin cannot absorb degradation or scatter.
W = π σ_a ε_a sin δ per cycle; power = W × frequency; adiabatic rate = power/(ρc). Accelerate by frequency only with temperature measured and a 1 Hz check.
Wet 37 °C environment, several amplitude levels, unloaded and static-load controls, stiffness, porosity and flow measured, stopping criteria and run-outs fixed in advance.
A uniform downward load w over span L has resultant wL acting at the midpoint.
With downward load positive and the lesson convention, dV/dx=−w; the shear change is the negative signed load area.

cards.front: Shear jump at a point force
cards.back: A downward point force P causes a downward jump of magnitude P in V; M remains continuous across a finite force.
dM/dx=V; the signed area under the shear diagram gives the change in bending moment.
Check interval boundaries and interior points where V=0; then apply the stated stress model and verify units.

cards.front: Poisson's ratio and generalized Hooke's law
cards.back: Lateral strain = −ν × axial strain. ε_x = [σ_x − ν(σ_y + σ_z)]/E; volumetric strain = (1 − 2ν)(σ_x + σ_y + σ_z)/E.
Holding ε_y = 0 under σ_x gives σ_y = νσ_x. A material constrained laterally is effectively stiffer.
Free heating: ε = αΔT, no stress. Fully constrained: σ = −EαΔT. With a gap, only the expansion beyond the gap is suppressed.
Cylinder: σ_θ = pr/t, σ_z = pr/(2t). Sphere: pr/(2t). Valid for r/t ≥ 10. Radius growth Δr = r(σ_θ − νσ_z)/E for a cylinder.
For a rectangle I = bh³/12, so a 25% deeper section has about 1.95 times the second moment of area and deflects about half as much under the same load.

cards.front: Strong enough is not stiff enough
cards.back: Apply the stress and deflection criteria separately; a beam far below its stress limit can still exceed a deflection limit.
In a linear model, scale the applied load by limit ÷ current value for each criterion; the smaller of the two loads governs the allowable load.

cards.front: Why are equilibrium equations insufficient for a redundant reaction?
cards.back: Deformation compatibility and a constitutive/stiffness model supply an additional relation beyond whole-structure force and moment balance.

cards.front: Which conditions define the unilateral prop?
cards.back: Nonnegative upward reaction, nonnegative gap and zero reaction-times-gap, with gap and displacement directions explicitly defined.

cards.front: How should a beam moment diagram be checked?
cards.back: Verify cut-section signs, endpoints, shear jumps, dM/dx=V, dV/dx=−w and units rather than relying on a plausible drawing.

cards.front: Can average stiffness be substituted freely in an indeterminate beam?
cards.back: No. Flexibilities depend on weighted stiffness integrals; a nominal average may change redundant reaction sharing.

cards.front: Can yield strength alone predict permanent set?
cards.back: No. A post-yield/unloading law and a loading history are required in addition to a yield value.

cards.front: Which energy is recovered in elastic unloading of the ideal bar?
cards.back: The elastic strain-energy portion. The model’s plastic work is not recovered by the same unloading line.

cards.front: What determines load sharing after one parallel member yields?
cards.back: Compatibility plus each material’s current constitutive branch; the tangent stiffness changes as the history changes.

cards.front: Why must unloading specify force versus displacement control?
cards.back: Returning external force to zero and returning the assembly to zero displacement generally impose different final conditions and residual states.

cards.front: What should be rechecked after a support settlement changes a reaction?
cards.back: Recompute the other reactions and internal fields, then verify displacement compatibility, equilibrium and the admissible contact state.

cards.front: What makes contact-state selection more than an equilibrium calculation?
cards.back: It adds inequality and complementarity constraints; an algebraic reaction can satisfy balance while violating the declared support’s allowed action.

cards.front: Which independent ledgers should this material report close?
cards.back: The strain decomposition, force/stress relation and work/recoverable/plastic-energy partition, each under the declared control and constitutive assumptions.

cards.front: Can zero external force imply a nonzero residual extension?
cards.back: Yes. Compatible material histories can leave permanent common strain and self-equilibrated internal stresses after the external resultant is removed.
